title: Summer and Garden
premise: Oscar Eastwick, a once-promising cellist whose hands failed him during a career-defining concert, retreats to the island town of Bellhaven to teach music and avoid feeling anything. When his imperious grandmother summons the family for one last summer at Eastwick House before she sells it, Oscar hires Marisol Vega, the ferry mechanic who once fixed his car at midnight, to pose as his partner for the weekend. The fake date works too well: Marisol's warmth cracks Oscar's defenses, while the family reunion unearths the truth that Oscar's father sabotaged his career to keep him home, and that Oscar's grandmother is selling the house to protect a secret inheritance meant for Oscar all along. As the last ferry of the season approaches, Oscar must forgive himself for the collapse, choose Marisol for real, and decide whether Eastwick House is a prison or a home.
about_author: Wendell Brightwater is the pen name of a former orchestra librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's music before writing about the players. They live on a cold coast with a dog named Fermata and a garden that only blooms out of spite.

chapters.title: The Muscle That Lies
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Two years after the disastrous final performance, Oscar teaches cello to bored teenagers in Bellhaven and insists the heart is trainable, containable. A letter from grandmother Odile summons the family for the house's last summer. Beat: numbness dressed up as discipline.

chapters.title: Midnight at the Ferry Dock
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol, who keeps the island's boats running and her own past locked in a toolbox, remembers fixing a stranger's car in the rain two years ago. That stranger, Oscar, walks back into her life asking for an impossible favor. Beat: curiosity overriding caution.

chapters.title: Terms and Conditions
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Over bad coffee, Oscar proposes the fake-dating arrangement: one weekend, one performance, no feelings. Marisol names a price—Oscar's grandmother's neglected garden, which she wants to restore. Beat: a contract both of them already intend to break.

chapters.title: First Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. They rehearse their romance in Marisol's boathouse, trading invented first-date stories that keep sounding real. Oscar's hands shake when Marisol asks about the concert; she pretends not to notice. Beat: intimacy disguised as practice.

chapters.title: The House That Remembers
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Arrival at Eastwick House: Odile's imperious welcome, siblings Theo and Camille circling like gulls, and the garden gone to seed—a wound Oscar doesn't understand yet. Marisol plays her role perfectly. Beat: dread wearing party clothes.

chapters.title: Too Real by Dessert
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The reunion dinner turns vicious when Theo mocks Oscar's failure. Marisol defends Oscar with a story so tender it silences the table—and startles them both. In the garden afterward, a near-kiss. Beat: the fake date stops being fake.

chapters.title: Camille's Ledger
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Camille, the family accountant, hints that the house's sale isn't about money. Odile watches Oscar's hands across the room and says, 'You used to play for me.' Oscar flees to the boathouse. Beat: the past knocking.

chapters.title: What the Garden Grew
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Working the soil, Marisol unearths a rusted tin box of clippings about Oscar's concert and a letter Odile never sent. Marisol hides it, torn between loyalty and honesty. Beat: knowledge as a burden.

chapters.title: The Storm Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A storm traps everyone indoors; Theo forces a family performance. Oscar's hands seize up in front of everyone—until Marisol sits beside him and turns it into a duet of humming and rhythm. Beat: humiliation transformed, almost.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. After the storm, in the boathouse, Oscar and Marisol finally kiss. Then Oscar panics, invoking the contract's terms, and Marisol, hurt, agrees to keep it professional. Beat: the heart refusing to stay containable.

chapters.title: Theo's Gambit
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Theo reveals he knows Marisol is being paid and threatens to expose the arrangement—unless Oscar signs away any claim to the house. Oscar realizes the inheritance fight is the real reunion. Beat: blackmail in linen shirts.

chapters.title: The Tin Box
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Guilty, Marisol returns the box to Oscar's room and confesses she found it. Oscar reads Odile's unsent letter: an apology for what the family did to Oscar's mother, and to Oscar. Beat: grief with a return address.

chapters.title: The Father Question
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Flashback chapter: the night of the catastrophic concert, and the dawning suspicion that Oscar's father's 'encouragement' was sabotage. Oscar confronts the mirror: the collapse wasn't only the hands. Beat: self-blame cracking.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confronts Oscar about running—from the stage, from her, from the truth. Oscar, cornered, says something unforgivable about Marisol's own past, which she has never explained. Beat: the fake relationship detonating for real.

chapters.title: Marisol's Harbor
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol tells Oscar her story: a childhood of foster homes, a brother lost to the sea, why she fixes boats—so nothing she loves drifts away. Oscar listens without fixing anything. Beat: the first honest conversation.

chapters.title: Odile's Confession
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Odile reveals the secret: the house was always meant for Oscar, held in trust against the father's schemes; the sale was leverage to force the family to face each other. She asks Oscar's forgiveness for staying silent. Beat: inheritance redefined.

chapters.title: The Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol decides to leave on the last ferry—she won't be anyone's arrangement. Oscar races the dock, and instead of a speech, plays cello on the pier, hands steady for the first time in two years. Beat: the climax; love as performance made real.

chapters.title: What Oscar Forgave
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar forgives the person in the mirror: the collapse, the running, the cruelty to Marisol. A quiet chapter of repair—apology accepted, not instantly, but truly. Beat: forgiveness as work, not feeling.

chapters.title: The Vote
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The family gathers to decide the house's fate. Oscar refuses Theo's deal, accepts the inheritance, and proposes Eastwick House become a summer music school—with Marisol's garden as its heart. Beat: power chosen over power refused.

chapters.title: Turning the Soil
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Weeks later, Marisol returns—not as an arrangement but by choice. She and Oscar plant the garden together, arguing happily about roses versus vegetables, while Odile supervises from a lawn chair. Beat: found family taking root.

chapters.title: First Recital
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The music school's first recital in the restored garden: Oscar's students play, Camille keeps the books, Theo, chastened, hauls chairs. Oscar performs again—imperfect, alive, unafraid. Beat: the career that mattered was never the one that ended.

chapters.title: Summer, and Garden
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, closing scene. A year later, on the anniversary of the reunion, Oscar and Marisol sit in the garden as the last ferry of the season sounds its horn and neither of them needs it. Beat: staying, chosen freely, as the story's final answer.
